signal.title: [data] ds.summary() crashes on boolean columns with ArrowNotImplementedError
signal.text: ## What happened + What you expected to happen `ds.summary()` crashes with `ArrowNotImplementedError` when the dataset contains boolean columns. **Expected**: `summary()` should handle boolean columns without crashing. ## How to reproduce ```python import pyarrow as pa import pyarrow.compute as pac bool_array = pa.array([True, False, True]) mean = pac.mean(bool_array).as_py() pac.subtract(bool_array, mean) # ArrowNotImplementedError: no kernel for subtract(bool, double) pac.quantile(bool_array, q=0.5) # ArrowNotImplementedError: no kernel for quantile(bool) pac.equal(bool_array, 0) # ArrowNotImplementedError: no kernel for equal(bool, int64) ``` ## Root cause In `stats.py`, `DataType.bool()` is mapped to `_numerical_aggregators`, which includes all 8 numeric aggregators. Three of them crash on boolean columns because PyArrow has no kernels for the underlying operations: | Aggregator | Operation | Error | |---|---|---| | `Std` | `pac.subtract(bool, double)` in `arrow_block.py:sum_of_squared_diffs_from_mean` | `no kernel for subtract(bool, double)` | | `ApproximateQuantile` | `pac.quantile(bool)` in `arrow_block.py:quantile` | `no kernel for quantile(bool)` | | `ZeroPercentage` | `pc.equal(bool, int64)` in `aggregate.py:aggregate_block` | `no kernel for equal(bool, int64)` | Only `Count`, `Mean`, `Min`, `Max`, and `MissingValuePercentage` work on booleans. ## Suggested fix Give `DataType.bool()` its own aggregator list that excludes `Std`, `ApproximateQuantile`, and `ZeroPercentage`. ## Versions / Dependencies Ray 2.46+
signal.author: ashutosh1807

signal.title: [Serve] Name the label selector when replicas cannot be scheduled
signal.text: ## Description When a replica cannot be scheduled because no node satisfies its `label_selector`, the slow-startup warning reports only resources, so it shows ample free capacity and points at autoscaling or runtime env setup instead. We hit this in production: a replica sat pending for 15 minutes while the message read `Resources required for each replica: {"CPU": 1.0}, total resources available: {"CPU": 800.0}`. Hundreds of nodes had free CPU; none carried the labels the selector had just been changed to. This names the label_selector: ``` ... or for a node matching the replica's label selector to become available. Resources required for each replica: {"CPU": 1.0}, total resources available: {"CPU": 800.0}. Required node label selector: {"test": "in(test-1, test-2, test-3)"}. ... ``` Deployments without a selector are unaffected; the sentence is omitted. ## Related issues ## Additional information Message text only, no behavior change. Verified on a two-node cluster (ample CPU, no matching node) -- the output above is actual. Unit tests cover the selector-present and selector-absent paths.

signal.title: [core][uv] Keep the command intact when it has "--option=value" arguments
signal.text: ## Description `uv run` currently breaks whenever the first argument of the wrapped command is written as `--option=value`. The runtime env hook has to split the driver's command line into the part that belongs to `uv run` and the part that is the actual command. It does that by parsing the command line with an `optparse` parser that knows the `uv run` options, treating the first argument the parser doesn't recognize as the start of the command, and then recovering the `uv run` arguments by subtracting the length of that command from the original command line. That subtraction assumes the command handed back by `_parse_args` is a suffix of the arguments it was given. It isn't, when the first unrecognized argument uses the `--option=value` form: `optparse._process_long_opt` pops the argument, splits it at the `=`, pushes the bare `value` back onto the remaining arguments, and *only then* reports the option as unknown. The command therefore comes back one entry longer than the slice it is measured against, and the `uv run` arguments are cut one argument short: | command line | `uv_run_args` before | `uv_run_args` after | | --- | --- | --- | | `uv run -m ray.util.client.server --address=h:p` | `uv run -m` | `uv run -m ray.util.client.server` | | `uv run -m ray.util.client.server --address h p` | `uv run -m ray.util.client.server` | unchanged | | `uv run --model=x script.py` | `uv` | `uv run` | The truncated `uv run -m` then reaches the `argparse` call just below, which fails with the error from the issue: ``` usage: __main__.py [-h] [--directory DIRECTORY] [-m MODULE] __main__.py: error: argument -m/--module: expected one argument ``` Ray Client passes every argument of its server in the `--option=value` form (`--address=...`, `--host=...`, `--port=...`, `--mode=...`), so `uv run` combined with Ray Client fails this way every time. ## Related issues Fixes #62650 ## Additional information `_parse_args` now returns a command that is always a suffix of the arguments it was given, by locating the unrecognized argument in the original list instead of rebuilding it from `err.opt_str`. The caller then derives the boundary directly from the command's length, which removes the `original_length`/`args_consumed` bookkeeping. Two details worth flagging for review: - Prepending `err.opt_str` cannot recover the original argument, because after the exception the remaining arguments look identical for `--address=h:p` and `--address h:p`. So the boundary is decided by checking whether the original argument at that position is exactly `f"{err.opt_str}={rargs[0]}"`. Comparing the whole reconstructed argument rather than using `startswith` matters for a case like `--model --model=x`, where the *value* of a space-separated unknown option itself looks like `option=value`. - `_parse_args` now copies the list it is given instead of parsing it in place, so the caller no longer has to snapshot its length before parsing. ### Testing - `test_uv_run_parser` gains the `--option=value` forms, including an empty value, an unknown option in that form directly after `uv run`, and the `--model --model=x` case above. - `test_uv_run_runtime_env_hook_option_with_equals` is a new test covering the reported failure at the `hook()` level, using a Ray Client style command line. It stubs `_get_uv_run_cmdline`, so it needs neither a cluster nor a real `uv` process. Both tests fail on master (the new one with the exact `argument -m/--module: expected one argument` above) and pass with this change: ``` $ pytest python/ray/tests/test_runtime_env_uv_run.py -k "test_uv_run_parser or option_with_equals" 2 passed, 8 deselected ``` I also replayed every command line the existing tests in this file use through the old and the new boundary logic and confirmed they agree on all of them, so the change only affects the `--option=value` case that was broken. `ruff check`, `ruff format` and `pydoclint` are clean on both files. The other tests in this file need a Ray cluster or a real `uv` subprocess, which my sandbox can't provide (`psutil.pids()` is blocked), so I'm relying on CI for those.

signal.title: [Job] Retry transient RPC errors in job monitor during GCS failover
signal.text: Description： During GCS HA failover (kill head pod), the job monitoring loop in dashboard_agent receives gRPC CANCELLED/UNAVAILABLE errors. The current except Exception handler does not distinguish transient errors from permanent failures, immediately marking jobs as FAILED — even though the Driver process and Worker Actors remain alive on the worker node. This is inconsistent with how other Ray components handle GCS disconnections: - Raylet (C++): has NotifyGCSRestart reconnection mechanism - CoreWorker (C++): has automatic reconnection - job_manager.py (Python): no retry ← this PR fixes it Changes: - Add _is_transient_rpc_error() to identify CANCELLED (code 1) and UNAVAILABLE (code 14) gRPC errors - Wrap get_status() in try/except — if GCS is also unreachable and error is transient, retry - If get_status() succeeds but original error is transient, retry instead of marking FAILED - Exponential backoff: min(2^n, 30)s, max 40 attempts (~20min) - Reset retry counter on successful supervisor ping - Add unit test for _is_transient_rpc_error() helper Configurable via RAY_JOB_MONITOR_MAX_TRANSIENT_ERROR_RETRIES env var (default 40). Related issues Fixes #65025 Additional information - Verified on a production GCS HA cluster with a high-frequency actor workload (256 actors batch create/kill) - Kill head pod → job stays RUNNING → GCS recovers → monitoring resumes - Non-transient errors still immediately mark FAILED (no behavior change) - Test: pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/tests/test_job_manager.py::test_job_monitor_retries_transient_rpc_errors -v

signal.title: [core][rdt] Upgrade NIXL to v1.4.0
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Upgrades NIXL from `1.3.1` to `1.4.0` in the `ray[llm]` extra. `python/setup.py` (`setup_spec.extras["llm"]`) and `python/requirements/llm/llm-requirements.txt` are paired source-of-truth files and are updated together, along with the four regenerated `python/deplocks/llm/*.lock` files. Note that this pin now runs ahead of vLLM's `requirements/kv_connectors.txt`, which the requirements file says to keep NIXL in sync with: vLLM `v0.26.0` (the version Ray pins) requires `nixl==1.3.1` and vLLM `main` is at `1.3.2`. This is not a resolver conflict, since `kv_connectors.txt` is an optional requirements file rather than part of vLLM's `install_requires`, and the depsets compile cleanly. `python/requirements/ml/dl-gpu-requirements.txt` still pins `nixl==0.4.0` for the core GPU CI image that runs the RDT NIXL tests. That is a separate dependency set and is intentionally untouched here. ## Related issue number N/A — dependency version bump. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "nixl"` returns 17 open NIXL/RDT PRs; none of them changes the pinned NIXL version. This PR previously targeted `1.3.1`, which has since landed on master through another change, so the original diff had become empty and is replaced here by the `1.4.0` bump. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] Testing Strategy - [x] This PR is not tested :( — dependency pin bump, covered by existing CI. Run locally on macOS/arm64, rebased on master at `01a34b54e0`: - `bazelisk run //ci/raydepsets:raydepsets -- build ci/raydepsets/configs/rayllm.depsets.yaml` — all 8 depsets compiled successfully. - `bazelisk run //ci/raydepsets:raydepsets -- build ci/raydepsets/configs/rayllm.depsets.yaml --check` — "Lock files are up to date." - `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` — all hooks passed. - Lock diff reviewed: only the `nixl` / `nixl-cu13` version and hash lines changed, with no collateral version drift in any other package. Not run locally: the LLM GPU / RDT NIXL suites, which need CUDA GPUs on a Linux image. Runtime behavior of the 1.4.0 wheel is relying on CI. signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_metrics suites on constrained CI runners
signal.text: The eternal test_metrics/_2/_3 targets fail repeatedly on unrelated PRs when runners are memory-starved (/dev/shm ~2.6GB warnings, OOM worker deaths): a different test fails each attempt, always as a metric-export wait timeout or an empty Prometheus scrape ("Available metrics: []"), never a wrong value. - metrics_start_shutdown: cap object_store_memory at 500MB. The default 30%-of-RAM sizing overflows /dev/shm on constrained runners and silently falls back to disk-backed /tmp, slowing the whole cluster past the tests waits and adding OOM pressure. Pin num_cpus=16 so scheduling does not depend on the runner core count (mirrors _shared_serve_instance). - metrics_start_shutdown: after serve.start, wait (best-effort) for the controller control-loop gauge from the current session to appear in a scrape, proving the Serve actor -> agent -> endpoint pipeline is live before test bodies assert on metrics. - Lengthen the shortest first-appearance metric waits (5-15s) in the tests seen failing: first export on a loaded machine routinely exceeds them. - get_metric_dictionaries: distinguish "metric missing" from "scrape returned nothing at all" in the failure message.

signal.title: [autoscaler] Fix floating-point formatting in resource usage display
signal.text: Fixes #42491 ## Description This PR improves the formatting of resource usage values displayed in Ray autoscaler output (`ray status` and related utilities). Previously, floating-point precision artifacts (e.g. `0.010000000000000009`) could appear in resource usage output. This change introduces a `format_resource()` helper to normalize numeric values into human-readable strings by removing floating-point noise while preserving precision where needed. The updated formatting is applied consistently across: - `parse_usage()` (resource usage display) - placement group resource reporting - node type resource summaries Additionally, tests were added to validate correct formatting behavior and ensure consistent output across edge cases. ## Key changes - Added `format_resource()` utility using Python’s `g` format specifier - Updated `parse_usage()` to format: - used / total resource values - placement group resource values - Updated node type formatting output for consistency --- ## Test coverage Added tests: - `test_format_resource()` → validates float formatting edge cases - `test_parse_usage_formatting()` → ensures consistent formatted output across CPU, memory, and custom resources ## Example improvement Before: 0.010000000000000009/1 special_hardware After: 0.01/1 special_hardware ## Impact This change improves readability of `ray status` output without affecting functionality or resource accounting logic.

signal.title: [data] A fast upstream actor pool can starve a slow-starting downstream bottleneck
signal.text: ### What happened + what I expected Think of a streaming pipeline as two workers sharing the same toolbox: - **Robber** is the upstream stage. It starts quickly, takes as many CPU slots as it can, and can fill the next queue faster than that queue drains. - **Bottleneck** is the downstream stage. It is slightly slower per item and its actors take time to initialize, so it determines total pipeline throughput. Once Bottleneck has a queue, giving Robber more CPUs does not help end-to-end throughput. Those CPUs are more valuable at Bottleneck. With 128 CPUs and one CPU per actor, this simple example uses 126 CPUs for the two actor stages. Their service times are 0.17s and 0.21s. Balancing their rates gives approximately: ``` robber_workers / 0.17 = bottleneck_workers / 0.21 robber_workers + bottleneck_workers = 126 robber_workers ~= 56 bottleneck_workers ~= 70 ``` Ray Data does not need to know this exact answer in advance. I expected its default autoscaling to remain work-conserving and react when Bottleneck has thousands of queued inputs. Instead, one repeated default run reached **83 Robber actors and only 4 Bottleneck actors (3 running, 1 pending)** while Bottleneck had **6,190 queued blocks**. Only 86 of 128 CPUs were active. When Robber finished, Bottleneck still had only 7 actors with 13,788 queued blocks, and only 27 CPUs were active. This made the default pipeline more than twice as slow as simply giving both autoscaling pools throughput-balanced initial sizes. `initial_size` is only a starting point; normal autoscaling remains enabled. | Ray 2.57 configuration | Repeated E2E time | | --- | ---: | | Default `ActorPoolStrategy()` | 196.5–199.7s | | `initial_size=56` then `initial_size=70` | 92.6–98.5s | | Fixed 56 then 70 (control only) | 90.7–92.9s | This reproduction has no fanout or repartition operator. The input is materialized before the timer, every physical block contains one row, and every stage processes one row at a time. ### Standalone reproduction Run each mode in a fresh process: ```bash MODE=balanced python repro.py MODE=default python repro.py ``` ```python import os import time import ray import ray.data NUM_ITEMS = 14_543 NUM_CPUS = 128 class Robber: def __init__(self, seconds): self.seconds = seconds def __call__(self, batch): assert len(batch["id"]) == 1 time.sleep(self.seconds) return batch class Bottleneck: def __init__(self, seconds, init_seconds): self.seconds = seconds time.sleep(init_seconds) def __call__(self, batch): assert len(batch["id"]) == 1 time.sleep(self.seconds) return batch def sink(batch): assert len(batch["id"]) == 1 return batch mode = os.environ.get("MODE", "default") if mode not in {"default", "balanced"}: raise ValueError("MODE must be default or balanced") ray.init(num_cpus=NUM_CPUS, include_dashboard=False) # Source construction is deliberately outside the timed pipeline. source = ray.data.range( NUM_ITEMS, override_num_blocks=NUM_ITEMS, ).materialize() assert source.num_blocks() == NUM_ITEMS if mode == "balanced": robber_compute = ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy(initial_size=56) bottleneck_compute = ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy(initial_size=70) else: robber_compute = ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy() bottleneck_compute = ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy() output = ( source .map_batches( Robber, batch_size=1, batch_format="numpy", compute=robber_compute, fn_constructor_args=(0.17,), num_cpus=1, ) .map_batches( Bottleneck, batch_size=1, batch_format="numpy", compute=bottleneck_compute, fn_constructor_args=(0.21, 8.0), num_cpus=1, ) .map_batches( sink, batch_size=1, batch_format="numpy", num_cpus=1, ) ) started = time.perf_counter() result = output.materialize() elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started assert result.num_blocks() == NUM_ITEMS assert result._block_num_rows() == [1] * NUM_ITEMS print(f"{mode}: {elapsed:.2f}s") ``` The 8-second constructor is synthetic, but represents ordinary actor setup such as importing a model or initializing a GPU-backed stage. The reproduction itself uses CPUs only. ### Working theory This looks like an interaction between fair-share resource allocation and actor-pool ramp-up: 1. Robber starts quickly and grows to most of the useful actor capacity. 2. Bottleneck starts from a small pool. In the slow period above, it was observed with approximately one pending constructor at a time despite a large input queue and many idle CPUs. 3. When Robber drains, Bottleneck cannot acquire initialized actors quickly enough, so the cluster becomes non-work-conserving. That diagnosis is an inference from the executor logs, not a proposed requirement to always prioritize downstream operators. Any fix should preserve Ray Data's memory backpressure and avoid over-creating expensive actors. The narrower expected property is: when a downstream actor operator has substantial runnable work and available resource budget, actor initialization and cross-operator allocation should not leave most shared resources idle for a long time. ### Related issues - #65433 covers task-pool operators overstating currently runnable demand. A no-op task sink can interact with this reproduction, but it does not explain the slow downstream actor ramp by itself. - #65473 covers per-output delivery overhead for one-row fanout. This reproduction has no fanout or repartition, so it isolates a separate resource-allocation/autoscaling problem. ### Versions Reproduced twice on Ray 2.57.0, commit `4464bbb6e21bce4893ed3396b2e33996188d511d`, on a single 128-CPU host. ### Issue severity High for streaming actor pipelines with expensive setup: execution is correct and eventually finishes, but default scheduling can more than double end-to-end time while leaving substantial compute capacity idle.

signal.title: [Data] map_batches/iter_batches streaming read holds 2-5x the dataset's uncompressed size as RSS, invisible to Ray's own object-store/task accounting
signal.text: ## What happened + What you expected to happen Reading a Parquet dataset via `ray.data.read_parquet(...).iter_batches()` or `.map_batches()` holds real (anonymous) process memory well beyond the size of the data — 2-5x the uncompressed dataset size in our measurements — while Ray's own accounting (object store usage, task/queued-block counters) stays under 1 GiB the whole time. An equivalent plain-pyarrow streaming scan (`pyarrow.parquet.ParquetFile.iter_batches`) of the same file stays close to the file's actual size. This matters because it makes Ray Data's real memory footprint impossible to predict from anything Ray itself reports: the object store, task counters, and block sizes all look fine while the process is actually using several times that much RSS. On a memory-constrained worker (e.g. an 8 GiB pod), this causes an OOM kill that nothing in Ray's own metrics predicted or explained. We first found this on Ray 2.56 doing a byte-for-byte layer-by-layer bisect (isolated pyarrow scan vs. Ray `count()`/`iter_batches()`/`map_batches()` on the same file, matched versions, no other library in the picture). It reproduces just as clearly on a from-scratch synthetic dataset (no external files/services), and **it still reproduces on 2.57.0**, released 2026-08-11 — we re-ran the isolated repro on both macOS and a Linux/EKS pod after upgrading to confirm before filing. ### Measurements **Linux (EKS pod, cgroup v2, 4 CPU / 8 GiB limit), Ray 2.57.0 / pyarrow 25.0.1** — 25M-row synthetic dataset, 1.19 GiB uncompressed on disk (uncompressed parquet, so file size ≈ in-memory row data size): | Read path | RSS overhead (Δ over baseline) | vs. pyarrow | Wall time | |---|---|---|---| | pyarrow `ParquetFile.iter_batches` | +0.75 GiB | 1.0x (baseline) | — | | Ray `Dataset.iter_batches()` | +1.61 GiB | **2.2x** | 48.1s | | Ray `Dataset.map_batches(identity)` | +2.71 GiB | **3.6x** | 78.3s | Ray's own reported object-store usage stayed under ~550 MiB throughout both Ray runs (see progress-bar output in the attached log) — nowhere close to the 1.6-2.7 GiB of real process memory actually held. **macOS (local, same script), Ray 2.57.0 / pyarrow 25.0.1** — same synthetic-data generator, 5 runs: pyarrow baseline noisy (0.05-0.71 GiB, macOS memory-compression artifact) but Ray's *absolute* overhead was consistently 1.2-3.6 GiB against a 1.19 GiB dataset — i.e. roughly 1-3x the raw data size regardless of the noisy baseline ratio. **Original bisect (Ray 2.56 / pyarrow 24, dev cluster, cgroup `memory.stat` decomposition)** — for reference, isolating this from block-size caps, concurrency limits, object-store sizing, and `prefetch_batches`: | Layer | Δ RSS | Notes | |---|---|---| | pyarrow scanner (`pre_buffer=True`) | 0.95 GiB (flat) | reads every row | | Ray `iter_batches` | 3.20 GiB | same rows | | Ray `iter_batches`, `prefetch_batches=0` | 3.52 GiB | rules out prefetch | | Ray `map_batches` | 5.34 GiB | production-shaped UDF pattern | A dataset-size sweep (4.55M / 9.10M / 18.20M rows) showed the overhead **saturates** rather than scaling with data size (0.97, 0.73, 0.36 GiB per million rows — sublinear), and a resource sweep (`num_cpus` 1/2/4, object store 1/2 GiB) showed it is **independent of object-store size** and only **weakly** concurrency-scaled — consistent with a large, roughly fixed-size working set inside the streaming executor rather than a leak proportional to dataset size or a spillable/object-store-accounted allocation. ### Ruled out - pyarrow itself / `pre_buffer` — isolated pyarrow scan stayed bounded regardless. - Prefetching (`prefetch_batches=0` didn't reduce it). - Object store sizing (no effect across a 1-2 GiB sweep). - Concurrency (`concurrency=1`, i.e. single task, balloons identically to the default). - Consumer-code shape (per-block UDF, generator-fed driver merge, no `materialize()`/`take_all()`/`to_pandas()`/`list()` anywhere in the calling code). ## Versions / Dependencies - Ray: 2.57.0 (also reproduced on 2.56.0/2.56.1; original bisect on 2.56) - pyarrow: 25.0.1 (also reproduced on pyarrow 24) - Python: 3.12.9 - OS tested: Amazon Linux 2023 (EKS, kernel 6.12.94, cgroup v2) and macOS (local) ## Reproduction script No external files, buckets, or services — generates its own synthetic Parquet file in a temp dir. ```python """Minimal repro: Ray Data streaming read holds far more RSS than an equivalent pyarrow scan, on purely synthetic data (no external files/buckets). Requires: pip install "ray[data]" pyarrow psutil numpy Usage: python ray_data_memory_repro.py """ import gc import os import tempfile import threading import time import numpy as np import psutil import pyarrow as pa import pyarrow.parquet as pq import ray ROWS = 25_000_000 # ~1.2 GiB on disk with the columns below def make_dataset(path): ids = np.arange(ROWS, dtype=np.int64) table = pa.table( { "id": pa.array(ids), "v1": pa.array(ids.astype(np.float64) * 1.5), "v2": pa.array(ids.astype(np.float64) * 2.5 + 0.1), "v3": pa.array(ids.astype(np.float64) % 97.0), # unique per row so dictionary encoding can't collapse it away "tag": pa.array(np.char.mod("row-%d-xxxxxxxx", ids)), } ) pq.write_table(table, path, compression="none", row_group_size=500_000) def process_tree_rss(proc): total = proc.memory_info().rss for child in proc.children(recursive=True): try: total += child.memory_info().rss except psutil.NoSuchProcess: pass return total def peak_rss_during(fn, proc, poll_s=0.01): gc.collect() baseline = process_tree_rss(proc) state = {"peak": baseline, "done": False} def poll(): while not state["done"]: state["peak"] = max(state["peak"], process_tree_rss(proc)) time.sleep(poll_s) t = threading.Thread(target=poll, daemon=True) t.start() fn() state["done"] = True t.join() return (state["peak"] - baseline) / (1024**3) # GiB def pyarrow_scan(path): for _ in pq.ParquetFile(path).iter_batches(batch_size=64_000): pass def ray_iter_batches(path): for _ in ray.data.read_parquet(path).iter_batches(batch_format="pyarrow"): pass def ray_map_batches(path): ds = ray.data.read_parquet(path).map_batches(lambda b: b, batch_format="pyarrow") for _ in ds.iter_batches(): pass def run_ray_case(fn, path, proc): ray.init( address="local", # ignore RAY_ADDRESS; always start a fresh isolated instance num_cpus=2, object_store_memory=1 * 1024**3, include_dashboard=False, ) delta = peak_rss_during(lambda: fn(path), proc) ray.shutdown() return delta def main(): proc = psutil.Process(os.getpid()) with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: path = os.path.join(tmp, "data.parquet") make_dataset(path) print(f"file on disk: {os.path.getsize(path) / 1024**3:.2f} GiB") pa_delta = peak_rss_during(lambda: pyarrow_scan(path), proc) print(f"pyarrow scan: +{pa_delta:.2f} GiB RSS") iter_delta = run_ray_case(ray_iter_batches, path, proc) print( f"ray iter_batches: +{iter_delta:.2f} GiB RSS ({iter_delta / pa_delta:.1f}x pyarrow)" ) map_delta = run_ray_case(ray_map_batches, path, proc) print( f"ray map_batches: +{map_delta:.2f} GiB RSS ({map_delta / pa_delta:.1f}x pyarrow)" ) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ## Issue Severity High: It blocks me from completing my task. (Drives OOM kills on memory-constrained workers with no warning from Ray's own memory accounting; we've had to build a separate bounded pyarrow-shard read/aggregate engine as a workaround for aggregation-shaped reads, but general transform/map pipelines have no such option today.)
signal.author: satyarao-epi

signal.title: [Data] Preserve schema for empty datasets in schema unification and to_pandas()
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? `Dataset.to_pandas()` (and schema propagation generally) drops columns for an empty dataset: ```python import pyarrow as pa, ray empty_ref = ray.put(pa.table([pa.array([], pa.int32())], ["apples"])) rd = ray.data.from_arrow_refs([empty_ref]) assert list(rd.to_pandas().columns) == ["apples"] # fails on master: columns == [] ``` Two layers cause this: 1. **Metadata layer**: `unify_block_metadata_schema()` / `unify_ref_bundles_schema()` skip blocks with `num_rows == 0`, so a dataset made *only* of empty blocks reports no schema — even though an empty Arrow table carries a perfectly valid one (as noted by @mango766 on the issue). This PR makes empty-block schemas a fallback when no non-empty block provides a schema; non-empty blocks still take precedence. 2. **Consumption layer**: `to_pandas()` builds its result from `iter_batches()`, which yields no batches for an empty dataset, so `PandasBlockBuilder.build()` produced a DataFrame with zero columns. This PR reconstructs columns and dtypes from the dataset schema, routing Arrow-backed schemas through the same `BlockAccessor.to_pandas()` path used for non-empty blocks so empty and non-empty results agree on dtypes. This supersedes #64721 (same fix for layer 2, closed by the stale bot after both bot-review comments had been addressed; GitHub would not allow reopening it). This PR carries those commits, rebased on current master, plus the new metadata-layer fix. ## Related issue number Fixes #59946 ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] I've run pre-commit formatting (`black==22.10.0` per repo pin) on changed files. - [x] Testing strategy: - Added `test_to_pandas_empty_dataset_preserves_columns` (Arrow-backed and pandas-backed empty datasets, dtype parity with non-empty datasets). - Added `test_unify_block_metadata_schema_all_empty_blocks` (fallback + precedence). - Ran locally against master with the Ray nightly wheel + `setup-dev.py` symlinks: - `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_util.py` → 39 passed - `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_arrow_block.py -k to_pandas` → 13 passed - Issue's exact repro passes. ### Notes for reviewers / AI-assistance disclosure - This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I have reviewed every changed line and run the tests above locally. - Duplicate-work check: no other open PR references #59946; the only prior PR was my own #64721, which this supersedes.

signal.title: [Data] Fix Dataset.summary() crash on boolean columns
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? `Dataset.summary()` crashes with `ArrowNotImplementedError` on any boolean column: ```python import ray ds = ray.data.from_items([{"b": True}, {"b": False}, {"b": True}]) ds.summary() # pyarrow.lib.ArrowNotImplementedError: # Function 'subtract' has no kernel matching input types (bool, double) ``` `DataType.bool()` was mapped to `_numerical_aggregators`, but `Std`, `ApproximateQuantile`, and `ZeroPercentage` rely on PyArrow kernels with no boolean implementation. I probed each default aggregator individually against a bool column on master: `Count`, `Mean`, `Min`, `Max`, `MissingValuePercentage`, and `ApproximateTopK` all work; `Std` and `ZeroPercentage` raise `ArrowNotImplementedError` (and a boolean quantile is not meaningful). This PR gives boolean columns a dedicated `_boolean_aggregators` set — count, mean (= fraction of true values), min, max, missing-value percentage, and approximate top-k with k=2 (true/false counts) — and routes boolean dtypes to it in the heuristic fallback path as well. ## Related issue number Fixes #62235 ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] Formatting checked with the repo-pinned `black==22.10.0`. - [x] Testing strategy: - Added `test_summary_boolean_column` (end-to-end regression: `summary()` on a bool column with nulls, asserting count/mean/min/max/missing_pct values). - Added `test_boolean_aggregators` unit test; updated the two existing expectations that encoded "boolean is numerical". - `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_dataset_stats.py` → 39 passed (run locally against master via Ray nightly wheel + `setup-dev.py` symlinks). ### Notes for reviewers / AI-assistance disclosure - This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I have reviewed every changed line and run the tests above locally. - Duplicate-work check: no open PR references #62235. @jiangxt2 commented intent to work on this on Jul 2 with the same root-cause diagnosis, but no PR has appeared in the ~7 weeks since; happy to defer or hand off if one is in progress.

signal.title: [Serve] Import jinja2 lazily and declare it in the serve extra
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? As of 2.57.0, `controller.py` imports `haproxy.py` unconditionally, and `haproxy.py` imported jinja2 at module scope — but jinja2 was never declared in Ray's metadata (`ray-haproxy` is a binary distribution with `requires_dist: None`, so nothing pulls it in). On a slim base image: ```bash docker run --rm python:3.13-slim bash -c \ 'pip install -q "ray[default,serve]==2.57.0" && python -c "from ray import serve"' # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'jinja2' ``` This PR applies both fixes suggested in the issue: 1. **Lazy import**: `from jinja2 import Environment` moves from module scope into `_generate_config_file_internal()` (its single use site), so a plain `import ray.serve` no longer requires jinja2 — it's only needed when HAProxy mode actually renders its config. 2. **Declare the dependency**: `jinja2` is added to the `serve` extra in `setup.py` (mirrored in `python/requirements.txt`), so it's present when HAProxy mode *is* used. The compiled lockfiles already pin `jinja2==3.1.6`, so no lock regeneration is needed. ## Related issue number Fixes #65507 ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] Formatting checked with the repo-pinned `black==22.10.0`. - [x] Testing strategy (run locally against master via Ray nightly wheel + `setup-dev.py` symlinks): - Added `test_import_serve_does_not_require_jinja2`: a subprocess blocks jinja2 via a meta-path finder, then imports `ray.serve` and `ray.serve._private.controller`. Fails on master (repro of the issue), passes with this change. - Verified the render path still works with jinja2 present: constructed `HAProxyApi` and called `_generate_config_file_internal()`; a full HAProxy config (~5 KB) renders through the now-lazy import. ### Notes for reviewers / AI-assistance disclosure - This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I have reviewed every changed line and run the checks above locally. - Duplicate-work check: no open PR references #65507; the issue is unassigned with no claims.

signal.title: [Data] Release dead actors from the actor pool so they can be replaced
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? With a fixed-size actor pool and `max_errored_blocks = -1`, an actor that dies mid-pipeline (e.g. `sys.exit(0)` inside the UDF) makes the pipeline **hang silently forever** (repro from #62746, verified on master: hangs indefinitely; with this PR it completes). Root cause, as diagnosed in the issue: - `refresh_actor_state` detects the actor as `DEAD` and `_update_rank` removes it from the scheduling heaps, so no new tasks are dispatched to it — but the entry stays in `_running_actors`. - The pool's `current_size()` therefore never drops, so for a fixed-size pool (`min_size == max_size`) the autoscaler never creates a replacement (`default_actor_autoscaler` only upscales when `current_size() < min_size()`). - With `max_errored_blocks = -1`, the failed block is ignored instead of aborting, leaving 0 schedulable actors, a non-empty queue, and no exception. The fix: - `refresh_actor_state` now releases definitively-`DEAD` actors from the pool (with a warning log); the autoscaler then scales the pool back up to its min size. Actors whose local state is `None` (unknown, possibly transient) are left in place, as before. - `on_task_completed` tolerates actors already released with tasks in flight — `_release_running_actor` has already reconciled the pool's counters for them. ## Related issue number Fixes #62746 ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] Formatting with the repo-pinned `black==22.10.0`. - [x] Testing strategy (run locally against master via Ray nightly wheel + `setup-dev.py` symlinks): - Issue's repro script (bounded by a watchdog alarm): **hangs on master**, completes with this PR — dead actors are released ("actor ... is dead; releasing it from the actor pool so it can be replaced") and replaced, and `materialize()` finishes with the errored blocks dropped. - Added `test_dead_actor_released_and_replaced_e2e`: size-1 pool, UDF exits once via `sys.exit(0)`, asserts the pipeline completes. Passes in ~7s (pre-fix it would hang into the 180s pytest timeout). - `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_actor_pool_map_operator.py` → 54 passed. ### Notes for reviewers / AI-assistance disclosure - This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I have reviewed every changed line and run the tests above locally. - Duplicate-work check: no open PR references #62746 and the issue has no comments. The issue author checked "willing to submit a PR" in April 2026 but none has appeared since; happy to defer if one is in progress.

Changelog

Sourced from sqlparse's changelog.

Release 0.6.0 (Aug 13, 2026)

Notable Changes

  • Drop support for Python 3.8 and 3.9. Python 3.10+ is now required.
  • IMPORTANT: Fixes a potential denial of service attack (DOS) in the lexer, which consumed CPU quadratically on statements containing many unclosed dollar-quoted literals or multiline comments (CVE-2026-59893). See the security advisory for details: https://github.com/andialbrecht/sqlparse/security/advisories/GHSA-prg7-hcfm-mfcr The vulnerability was discovered by EQSTLab, min8282 and 7thpark. Thanks for reporting!
  • IMPORTANT: Fixes a potential denial of service attack (DOS) when grouping deeply nested or very wide statements. Building a token group re-read the whole group on every step, so a small statement could keep a worker busy for a long time (CVE-2026-54284, pr848 by alhudz and tonghuaroot).
  • IMPORTANT: Fixes a potential denial of service attack (DOS) in format(sql, reindent=True), which consumed CPU quadratically on long lists of tuples. See the security advisory for details: https://github.com/andialbrecht/sqlparse/security/advisories/GHSA-cfqr-cjx5-5jcm
  • IMPORTANT: Fixes a potential denial of service attack (DOS) on statements that consist only of comments (CVE-2026-71491). See the security advisory for details: https://github.com/andialbrecht/sqlparse/security/advisories/GHSA-f2ff-p2ww-7p4p The vulnerability was discovered by @​sanktjodel. Thanks for reporting!
  • IMPORTANT: Backslashes are now escaped in the python and php output formats. Without escaping, SQL containing a backslash could break out of the generated string literal (CVE-2026-59894). See the security advisory for details: https://github.com/andialbrecht/sqlparse/security/advisories/GHSA-3496-9g83-7v6x The vulnerability was discovered by @​7thParkk. Thanks for reporting!

Enhancements

  • Modernize type annotations in top-level API functions using PEP 585 and PEP 604 syntax.
  • END FOR and END CASE are now recognized as keywords.

Bug Fixes

  • Statement splitting was rewritten on a stack-based architecture. This fixes splitting of statements with nested BEGIN ... END blocks (issue845).
  • Fix function grouping being skipped in CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT statements when the as keyword is lowercase (pr867 by Osamaali313).
  • Recognize ROW_FORMAT as a keyword so that ALTER TABLE ... ROW_FORMAT=... no longer merges the table name and the option into a single identifier (issue773, pr860 by apoorvdarshan).
  • Recognize MATERIALIZED as a keyword so it is parsed and formatted consistently in CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW statements (issue752, pr854 by

... (truncated)

  • a51df6d Measure reindent offsets backwards to avoid quadratic CPU use
  • 73d9ccd Update CHANGELOG

  • ef2012a Fix quadratic DoS in group_comments (GHSA-f2ff-p2ww-7p4p)

Release notes

Sourced from mlflow's releases.

v3.15.0

MLflow 3.15.0 includes several major features and improvements

Major New Features

  • 🧩 MCP Registry: A centralized catalog for registering, versioning, and sharing Model Context Protocol servers — with semantic-versioned configs, promotable aliases, tags, auto-discovered tools, and ready-made connection instructions for Claude Code and .mcp.json. Manage it from the UI, REST API, or Python!
  • 🤖 MLflow Assistant enhancements: The in-app AI assistant now supports multiple LLM providers (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenAI-compatible/Gateway endpoints) chosen from a single settings page, displays live per-session token usage and estimated cost in the composer, and is easier to set up — mlflow agent setup can enable it in one prompt, with API keys stored securely in the Gateway's LLM Connections.
  • 🗂️ Sharable table views: Save named views of the Runs table — capturing columns, order, widths, filters, and sort — and share them by URL.
  • ⚡ Proxy-less artifact upload/download via presigned URLs: Large artifact transfers can now bypass the tracking server and talk directly to cloud storage (e.g. S3) through presigned URLs, cutting server load and timeouts on big files. We fall back to proxied transfer automatically for backward compatibility.
  • 🖼️ Multi-modal attachments in LLM judges: {{ trace }} judges created with make_judge() can now see images captured in trace spans via a new get_span_image tool, which fetches attachments as base64 data URLs and passes them to multimodal models (Anthropic, Gemini, and OpenAI-compatible via litellm) — enabling evaluation of vision tasks, screenshots, and other visual content.

signal.title: [serve] Deflake test_recursive_cancellation_during_execution
signal.text: B`test_recursive_cancellation_during_execution` synchronizes on a fixed 0.5s sleep instead of on the state it requires. `Replica._on_request_cancelled` only cancels child requests that are pending assignment, so the test needs `inner` to be executing when the cancel lands. If `inner` is still pending assignment, its assignment task is torn down, so it never enters `send_signal_on_cancellation`, causing the test to fail with `GetTimeoutError`. Holding the only slot of `inner` to delay its assignment shows the margin is under half a second, the test passes with a 0.1s delay and fails at 0.45s, 1.0s and 2.0s. The fix is to have `inner` signal from inside its cancel-catching block and wait for that before cancelling, the same method that `test_cancel_sync_handle_call_during_execution` already uses. Its three `ray.get` waits also go from 10s to 20s. Test-only change.
signal.author: johntaylor-cell

signal.title: [docs][core] Document JVM signal conflicts with PyArrow HDFS
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? On Linux, PyArrow HDFS loads `libhdfs`, which embeds a HotSpot JVM in the Python process. HotSpot uses some `SIGSEGV` events as recoverable VM control flow, while Ray's CoreWorker installs an Abseil failure-signal handler that can interpret the same signal as a fatal native crash. The conflict can be established during handler installation and surface later as an intermittent JVM crash. This PR documents: - the symptoms and root cause of the Ray/PyArrow HDFS signal-handler conflict; - HotSpot signal chaining with `libjsig.so` as the preferred mitigation because it keeps Ray's native crash diagnostics enabled; - `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` as a fallback and its diagnostic trade-off; - the process-start timing requirement for `LD_PRELOAD` and a KubeRay configuration example; - discoverable entry points from the Ray Data and Ray Train HDFS documentation. Related to #36415. ## Duplicate-work check I reviewed #36415 and searched open PRs for the issue number, `libjsig`, and PyArrow/HDFS signal-handler documentation. I found no open PR covering this documentation work. #58984 is already merged and added `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER`, but it didn't document the option, its diagnostic trade-off, or HotSpot signal chaining. ## Validation Documentation checks: - `git diff --check` - `python -m pre_commit run --files doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `sphinx-lint --disable trailing-whitespace doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `./ci/lint/lint.sh documentation_style` (`0 errors, 0 warnings`) - Verified the linked Oracle signal-handling pages and #36415 return HTTP 200. - Validated the documented `find`/`LD_PRELOAD` shell snippet with the local OpenJDK 17.0.19 installation. Runtime validation behind the guidance: - Reproduced the unmitigated JVM termination and generated multiple `hs_err_pid*.log` files. - Completed 5,000- and 10,000-operation HDFS stress runs with `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` without reproducing the crash. - Completed a 5,000-operation HDFS stress run with only `libjsig.so` preloaded and Ray's handler left enabled. - Completed a separate 1,000-operation `libjsig.so` run, followed by a clean `ray.shutdown()` and process exit code 0. The full Sphinx documentation site wasn't built locally because the existing Python environment doesn't include the Ray documentation dependency set. The Read the Docs preview build provides full-site validation. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate the failure, draft the documentation, and run the validation commands. I reviewed every changed line and the reported test results.

signal.title: [core] Enable TCP keepalive on GCS<->Redis connections
signal.text: ## Description Idle GCS↔Redis flows get silently removed by NAT, proxies, load balancers, and managed-service gateways. The GCS only finds out on its next command, which then hangs until a timeout instead of failing fast — and on a managed Redis behind an LB with a 60–350s idle timeout, this is a routine event, not an edge case. This PR enables TCP keepalive on every external Redis socket, applied from a single place in `ConnectWithoutRetries` so that sync, async, Sentinel, Cluster-redirect, and cleanup connections all get the same policy before TLS, AUTH, or any command runs. Two knobs, deliberately decoupled: | Config | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | `redis_tcp_keepalive_interval_seconds` | `30` | Keeps an idle flow alive. Must stay **below** the shortest idle timeout on the network path. `0` disables keepalive entirely. | | `redis_tcp_keepalive_probes` | `9` | How many unanswered probes declare the connection dead, so detection ≈ `interval * (1 + probes)`. | These two need opposite tuning — probes must be frequent enough to keep a flow alive, while declaring a connection dead must be slow enough to ride out transient congestion. hiredis ties them together (`TCP_KEEPINTVL = interval/3`, `TCP_KEEPCNT = 3`, so dead at `2 * interval` ≈ 60s), so this PR overrides both on glibc Linux to get ~5 minutes instead. That margin matters because in-place reconnect has not landed yet: a connection declared dead escalates to a GCS crash once the request retry budget is exhausted (`RedisRequestContext::Run` → `RAY_LOG(FATAL)`, and the periodic health check's `RAY_CHECK_OK` in `gcs_server.cc`). The docs carry an explicit warning about this, and the default is chosen conservatively for the same reason. **Platform support.** Only glibc Linux honors the probe count, because hiredis guards `TCP_KEEPIDLE`/`TCP_KEEPINTVL`/`TCP_KEEPCNT` on `__GLIBC__`. On musl only `SO_KEEPALIVE` is applied and kernel defaults govern the timing; macOS applies the interval alone; Windows uses a system-fixed probe count. The code, the runtime log, the config comments, the docs, and the test guards all agree on this — the log prints the *effective* values, not the configured ones, so a post-mortem shows which applied. ## Related issues Related to #65298 (`[core][2/N] Reconnect to Redis in place when the connection drops`). **This is not a duplicate.** I checked the open PR list before starting: - `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "redis keepalive"` → no results - `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "tcp keepalive in:title,body"` → only unrelated dependabot PRs - `gh pr diff 65298 | grep -iE "keepalive|SO_KEEPALIVE|KEEPIDLE"` → **zero hits** #65298 is *recovery* (reconnect once a connection is known dead). This PR is *detection and prevention* (keep the flow alive; find out promptly when it isn't). They are complementary, and this PR does not implement or pre-empt any part of #65298. **Coordination note for reviewers:** #65298 is open and touches four of the same files (`redis_context.cc`, `redis_context.h`, `ray_config_def.h`, and `kuberay-gcs-ft.md`), so whichever lands second will need a rebase. Two specific follow-ups once #65298 merges: 1. The `{warning}` block added here ("Ray does not yet reconnect to Redis in place… the GCS process exits") becomes false and must be rewritten. 2. The `redis_tcp_keepalive_probes` default of 9 is conservative *because* a dead connection currently means a crash. With reconnect in place, a shorter detection window becomes safe and probably desirable. Happy to rebase on top of #65298 instead, or to hold this until it merges — reviewer's call. Builds on #64299 (`[core][1/N] Make RedisContext::Connect non-fatal on connection failure`), already merged: this PR relies on `Connect()` returning a `Status`, and extends the same contract by making configuration errors non-retryable.

signal.title: [dashboard] Safely skip unsupported process GPU utilization API
signal.text: ## Description Some third-party NVML-compatible libraries export 'nvmlDeviceGetProcessesUtilizationInfo' but terminate the calling process when the API is invoked. Because this happens in native code, Python exception handling cannot prevent the Reporter Agent from exiting. ## What changed - Detect incompatible PPU devices before calling the process utilization API. - Use strict, case-insensitive standalone 'PPU' name matching. - Skip the API per GPU index so compatible NVIDIA GPUs on mixed nodes continue reporting per-process SM utilization. - Fail closed for the current collection cycle when device detection fails, and retry detection on the next cycle. - Add 'RAY_SKIP_PROCESS_UTIL_API=true as a node-wide operator escape hatch. - Preserve process IDs, allocated GPU memory, and device-level metrics when process utilization is skipped. - Document the escape hatch and its metric impact. ## Related issues Fixes #65414 ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc.

signal.title: [util] annotate Pool.close/terminate/join as returning None
signal.text: ``ray`` ships a py.typed marker, so these unannotated methods are treated as untyped functions by type checkers. Any caller running mypy in strict mode gets ``` error: Call to untyped function "close" in typed context [no-untyped-call] ``` for the standard ``pool.close(); pool.join()`` teardown, which leaves downstream projects either sprinkling per-call ignores or disabling ``disallow_untyped_calls`` for the whole ``ray`` package. All three methods already return None on every path.
signal.author: jonasdedden

signal.title: [core] annotate cluster_resources/available_resources return types
signal.text: Both are ``@PublicAPI``/``@DeveloperAPI`` entry points re-exported as ``ray.cluster_resources`` and ``ray.available_resources``, and both are documented as returning 'a dictionary mapping resource name to the total quantity of that resource'. Because they carry no annotation and ``ray`` ships py.typed, a strict-mode caller gets ``` error: Call to untyped function "cluster_resources" in typed context ``` and the result is ``Any``, so ``ray.cluster_resources()["CPU"] >= 2`` is unchecked. The quantities are accumulated as numbers and the GCS reports fractional resources, hence ``float``.
signal.author: jonasdedden

signal.title: [core] Fix RemoveSubmittedTaskReferences abandoning the batch on a missing ID
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Fixes #65320. `ReferenceCounter::RemoveSubmittedTaskReferences` walks a batch of argument IDs and drops each one's submitted-task ref. When an ID is not found in `object_id_refs_`, it logs a warning and **returns**, skipping every remaining argument in the batch: ```cpp auto it = object_id_refs_.find(argument_id); if (it == object_id_refs_.end()) { RAY_LOG(WARNING) << "Tried to decrease ref count for nonexistent object ID: " << argument_id; return; // skips every remaining argument } ``` Every argument after the missing one keeps its `submitted_task_ref_count` (and `lineage_ref_count` when `release_lineage` is true). `RefCount()` never reaches zero for those objects, so `DeleteReferenceInternal` never runs — the plasma value stays pinned and the task spec stays pinned as lineage for the lifetime of the process. Both common callers pass `release_lineage=true`, so the lineage leak is the usual outcome. Every sibling batch loop in this same file treats a missing/ineligible entry as *skip-this-one* rather than *abandon-the-batch* — `ReleaseLineageReferences`, `FreePlasmaObjects`, and `PopAndClearLocalBorrowers` all use `continue`. `git blame` shows the `return` predates the wrapping `for` loop: it dates to when the function handled a single object (`e50aa99be1e`, 2019-12), and the loop was added two months later (`4c2de7be540`, 2020-02) without revisiting it — i.e. a refactor leftover, not a deliberate abort. This changes the `return` to `continue` so one missing ID no longer leaks the ref counts of every argument after it in the batch. ## Note on reachability / testing As the issue notes, under correct accounting this branch cannot fire (`EraseReference` is CHECK-gated on `RefCount() == 0`, which includes `submitted_task_ref_count`, so an entry with a live submitted ref is never erased). The branch only fires after an upstream double-decrement has already occurred — a bug class that has recurred (e.g. #56123, #18908). So this is defensive: when that situation does arise, it should degrade to "skip the bad ID and correctly release the rest" instead of leaking every subsequent object for the process lifetime, matching how the sibling loops already behave. Because this is a one-token change to match the file's existing convention, I did not add a dedicated test (constructing the missing-entry state requires reproducing an upstream double-decrement). Happy to add a targeted unit test if maintainers would prefer one — guidance welcome on the preferred way to set up that state in the reference-counter tests. ## Related issue number Closes #65320 ## Checks - [x] I've made sure the change is scoped to a single, self-contained fix matching the existing `continue`-on-skip convention used by the sibling loops in this file.

signal.title: [Core] Make public ObjectRef typing compatible with runtime refs
signal.text: ## Description `ray.types.ObjectRef[T]` is currently a separate dummy generic class, while Ray remote functions return the real `ray._raylet.ObjectRef[T]`. Static type checkers therefore reject valid annotations that use the public import path. This change re-exports the canonical runtime/stub `ObjectRef` from `ray.types` and adds positive and negative typing regressions. Generic type information remains intact, and no distributed runtime, object-store, scheduling, serialization, or reference-counting behavior is changed. This is not duplicate work: #53591 remains open, searches for open PRs mentioning `53591` or `ray.types.ObjectRef` returned no results, and the broad `ObjectRef typing`/`ObjectRef generic` matches were inspected and are unrelated. Historical PR #55566 added generic runtime stub support but did not unify the public `ray.types.ObjectRef` symbol. AI assistance was used. I reviewed every changed line, understand the public-type/runtime-type boundary, and accept responsibility for the change. ## Related issues Closes #53591 ## Additional information Testing: - `MYPYPATH=python .venv/bin/mypy --follow-imports=silent python/ray/tests/typing_files/check_typing_good.py` -> PASS - negative mypy fixture -> expected 7 errors, including rejection of `ObjectRef[str]` assigned to `ObjectRef[int]` - `PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python .venv/bin/pyright python/ray/tests/typing_files/check_typing_good.py` -> PASS - `PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python .venv/bin/pyright python/ray/tests/typing_files/check_typing_actor_async.py` -> PASS - all pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed Python files -> PASS - runtime alias plus `ray.put`/`ray.get` smoke test with the locally installed Ray 2.54 runtime -> PASS - `git diff --check` -> PASS Bazel verification was attempted with the repository-required Bazel 7.5.0 binary. `//python/ray/tests:test_typing` built successfully, but the local test harness did not reach the assertions because the hermetic Python toolchain did not include `mypy`. After injecting the repository-pinned typing dependencies, the harness loaded the locally installed Ray 2.54 package rather than a current-master Ray wheel and failed in `conftest.py` on the newer `rocksdb_gcs_test_enabled` symbol. These were environment setup failures rather than typing-test failures.

signal.title: [Data] Disallow min_rows_per_file with partitioned parquet writes
signal.text: ## Description `min_rows_per_file` can't guarantee a minimum file size with `partition_cols`: each block can be split across partition directories, and no single write task necessarily sees all rows of a partition. Per the maintainer decision in [#59485](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/59485), deprecate the combination instead of silently ignoring the hint. This follows up on [#53930](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/53930), where the combination works when each partition fits in one write task. To avoid a hard behavior break, passing both options now emits a `DeprecationWarning` and retains the existing behavior. Users who repartitioned by the partition columns can remove `min_rows_per_file` without changing the output layout. ## What changed? - Emit a `DeprecationWarning` when `write_parquet` is called with both non-empty `partition_cols` and `min_rows_per_file`. - Apply the same warning to the deprecated `num_rows_per_file` alias. - Keep `partition_cols=[]` allowed, since it doesn't enable partitioned writes. - Update the `write_parquet` docstring and Ray Data docs with the migration guidance. - Update the tests to verify the warnings, successful writes, the deprecated alias, and the empty-list edge case. ## Related issues Related to [#59485](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/59485)

signal.title: [autoscaler] Precompute SerializeToString keys to eliminate redundant serialization in scheduling loop
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? After merging #64175, benchmark testing showed that scaling to 3000 nodes (15000 tasks × 0.2 CPU + 30MB memory) still takes ~51 minutes. Profiling with py-spy revealed two independent hotspots in the scheduling loop: 1. **Pre-filter logic flaw** — fixed in #65171 (OR-across-dimensions → AND-within-shape/OR-across-shapes) 2. **Redundant `SerializeToString` calls** — fixed in this PR The `UnschedulableRequestCache.contains()` serializes each request via `SerializeToString(deterministic=True)` once per candidate node inside `try_schedule`, resulting in **N_nodes × M_requests** redundant serializations per scheduling round. For 15000 requests across 3000 nodes, this produces ~45M repeated protobuf serializations. ### Profiling evidence (py-spy, 30s sample during baseline run): - `contains()` in scheduler.py: **55% Own CPU** (7.77s / 14s) - `_audit_fork_safety` triggered by SerializeToString inside `contains()`: **18% Own CPU** (2.43s / 14s) - Combined: **73% of scheduler CPU** spent on redundant serialization ![py-spy top](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8b5b56bb-0f87-445c-a5c9-9346bd3ce0d9) ### Fix Precompute a `{id(request): bytes}` dictionary **once** before entering the scheduling loop, and pass it through `_sched_best_node` → `try_schedule`. The `UnschedulableRequestCache` interface is simplified to accept raw `bytes` keys directly. Includes a defensive `.get()` fallback: if a request is not in the precomputed dict, it falls back to on-the-fly serialization rather than raising a `KeyError`. ## Benchmark Cluster: 3000 max workers (1 CPU each), 15000 tasks × 0.2 CPU. | Condition | Time to 3000 nodes | |-----------|-------------------| | After #64175 (baseline) | ~51 min | | + #65171 only (pre-filter AND/OR) | ~18 min | | + #65171 + this fix combined | ~14 min | ## Related PRs - #64175 — baseline optimization that this PR builds on (benchmark results from that PR revealed this hotspot) - #65171 — parallel fix for pre-filter logic (independent, can merge in either order) ## Checks - [x] I've signed all my commits with DCO sign-off. - [x] I've run the existing tests — all pass. The `try_schedule` interface change is backward-compatible via `Optional` parameter with on-the-fly fallback. - [x] Changes are confined to `python/ray/autoscaler/v2/scheduler.py` (single file, low blast radius). - [x] No duplicate PR exists for this optimization (searched open PRs for SerializeToString, precompute, UnschedulableRequestCache — zero matches). - [x] AI assistance was used. I (human submitter) have reviewed every changed line and understand the change end-to-end.
signal.author: Jade07-1

signal.title: [core][gcs] Use UNLINK instead of DEL for Redis namespace cleanup
signal.text:
## Description GCS namespace cleanup deletes each GCS table hash with `DEL`. With `lazyfree-lazy-user-del` at its default (`no`), `DEL` frees the value inline on the Redis main thread, so removing a large namespace blocks every other client of that Redis instance for the whole duration of the free. KubeRay runs this from the Redis-cleanup Job before removing a RayCluster's finalizer, typically against a Redis instance still shared with live clusters. Measured on one 351 MB GCS-shaped hash, with an unrelated client pinging Redis from a **separate process**: | | `DEL` (before) | `UNLINK` (after) | |---|---|---| | Max PING RTT, unrelated client | **950–993 ms** | **0.55–2.19 ms** | | PINGs completed during cleanup | 3 (baseline rate predicts ~645) | matches baseline | | Cleanup wall time | 953–996 ms | **3.4–7.3 ms** | Quiet-baseline PING p99 is 0.62 ms, so `DEL` is ~1500× that and Redis serves ~0.5 % of its normal request rate for the duration. The stall scales with the size of the freed value; `UNLINK`'s main-thread cost does not. This PR switches the delete loop to `UNLINK` with an automatic fallback, and fixes two related problems found in the same function. ### 1. `UNLINK` with a capability probe `RedisDelKeyPrefixSync` issues one `UNLINK` per key when the server accepts it. Because Ray documents no minimum Redis version, and `UNLINK` can additionally be denied by ACL or removed via `rename-command`, a bare substitution is not safe: > `RedisRequestContext::RedisResponseFn` (`redis_context.cc:191`) treats *any* > error reply as transient. It retries `num_redis_request_retries` times and then > `RAY_LOG(FATAL)`s. On the async path, "ERR unknown command 'UNLINK'" is a > crashed cleanup process — and under KubeRay v1.0.0, a RayCluster whose > finalizer is never removed. So the capability check runs once on the **sync** connection, where an error reply is observable, against a probe key under the namespace prefix cleanup is about to delete (`RAY@__unlink_probe__`). Every outcome other than the integer reply `UNLINK` is specified to return — error reply, unexpected reply type, timeout, transport error — degrades to `DEL`, i.e. exactly today's behavior, with a `WARNING`. The probe brackets its own socket timeout with `redis_db_probe_timeout_milliseconds`. After `Connect()` the sync context is left at `{0, 0}` (block forever) by `RestoreRedisTimeout`, so without this a black-hole server would hang cleanup indefinitely. `RAY_redis_namespace_cleanup_use_unlink=0` forces `DEL` and skips the probe — an escape hatch for teardown scripts that must observe memory reclaimed before cleanup returns. ### 2. The cleanup `SCAN` passed no `COUNT` `SCAN MATCH RAY@*` with no `COUNT` uses Redis's default of 10, and `MATCH` filters *after* the scan, so cleanup cost scaled with the **whole keyspace**, not with the namespace. The in-tree scanner already gets this right (`RedisScanner::Scan` passes `COUNT maximum_gcs_storage_operation_batch_size`); the cleanup path was written separately and never picked it up. Measured with 200,000 unrelated keys sharing the instance and a 5-key namespace: | | before | after | |---|---|---| | `SCAN` round trips | 19,272 | **200** | | Cleanup wall time | 2441.7 ms | **121.8 ms** | | Server CPU in `SCAN` (`INFO commandstats`) | 188,669 µs | **84,205 µs** | Server CPU drops as well, so this is not trading server work for round trips — at `COUNT 10` the per-call overhead dominates the actual bucket scanning. ### 3. Cleanup is now idempotent A key reporting `0` deleted was counted as `num_failed`, and the function returned `num_failed == 0`. But `SCAN` only guarantees each key is returned *at least* once — a duplicate from a cursor rewind, or a concurrent cleanup, made a fully successful run return `False`, which KubeRay consumes directly (`sys.exit(1) if not cleanup_redis_storage(...)`). Keys already absent are now counted separately and reported in the log line; the function returns `true` unless the process aborted. Scan results are collected into a `flat_hash_set` so a duplicate is not deleted twice and then miscounted. ## Related issues Closes #65520 ## Additional information ### Operator-visible behavior change `UNLINK` reclaims memory on a background thread, so `used_memory` may not drop until slightly after cleanup returns — measured at ~350 MB still held on return, with `lazyfree_pending_objects` = 1. Documented in the KubeRay GCS-FT guide, along with the fact that `RAY_redis_namespace_cleanup_use_unlink=0` must be set in the **head group's** pod template `env`: KubeRay builds the Redis cleanup Job's pod from the head pod template (`buildRedisCleanupJob` →`buildHeadPod`), so the Job inherits it. ### Tests New `RedisDelKeyPrefixSyncTest` fixture in `redis_store_client_test.cc`, five cases, all asserting exact `INFO commandstats` deltas (every `Connect()` issues one `DEL DUMMY`, so only exact deltas prove which verb the delete loop used): - `UnlinkIsUsedByDefault` — `del` == 1, `unlink` == N + 1 (probe + one per key) - `FallsBackToDelWhenDisabled` — `del` == N + 1, `unlink` == 0 (probe skipped) - `NopermFallsBackToDel` — an ACL user with `+@all -unlink` exercises the real error-reply fallback path end to end - `CleanupIsIdempotent` — a second run over an empty namespace returns `true` - `OtherNamespacesSurvive` — guards both the `SCAN` pattern and the probe key `NopermFallsBackToDel` is gated on `INFO server` `redis_version >= 6`: the Windows CI server is tporadowski Redis 5.0.9, where `ACL SETUSER` is an unknown command — and on this connection an error reply aborts the process rather than failing an assertion. The gate parses the version rather than trial-running an ACL command, for the same reason. The fixture carries a `CAUTION` comment spelling this out for future test authors. `test_redis_cleanup` in `test_gcs_utils.py` now asserts the return value, the exact commandstats deltas (single-node mode only — cluster mode has no single `INFO` view), and a second idempotent cleanup. **Commands run and results:** ``` $ bazel test //src/ray/gcs/store_client/tests:redis_store_client_test PASSED (10 tests) $ bazel test //src/ray/gcs/store_client/tests:chaos_redis_store_client_test PASSED (new cases skip under REDIS_CHAOS) $ TEST_EXTERNAL_REDIS=1 pytest -sv python/ray/tests/test_gcs_utils.py -k redis_cleanup 2 passed, 9 deselected in 107.52s test_redis_cleanup[True] (cluster mode) test_redis_cleanup[False] (single node, exact commandstats assertions) $ pre-commit run --files All hooks passed. (shellcheck skipped: its env fails to build locally; no shell files are changed) ``` ### Benchmarks Against Ray's bundled Redis 7.2.3 (standalone, `lazyfree-lazy-user-del no`), both arms on the **same binary** with only `RAY_redis_namespace_cleanup_use_unlink` differing, one process per arm (`RayConfig` reads `RAY_*` env vars once per process), 3 runs per arm, on 2 × Xeon @ 2.20 GHz / 7 GB RAM / Linux.
Full benchmark report (per-run numbers, methodology, reproduction) #### Environment | | | |---|---| | Ray | master `c725548279` + this change, built from source | | Redis | 7.2.3 (Ray's bundled server), standalone, `lazyfree-lazy-user-del no` (default), `appendonly no`, `maxmemory-policy noeviction` | | Host | 2 × Intel Xeon @ 2.20 GHz, 7 GB RAM, no swap, Linux 7.0.0-1008-gcp | | Client | Python 3.10, redis-py 8.1.0 | `lazyfree-lazy-user-del` is left at its default `no`, so `DEL` really is synchronous in the baseline arm. That is the honest comparison: the point of the change is that Ray cannot assume the operator has flipped that server-side setting. #### Benchmark 1: Redis main-thread stall **Workload.** One GCS-shaped hash `RAYbench@NODE` with 1,000,000 fields × 256 B values — 351.6 MB, `hashtable` encoding (large enough that `lazyfreeGetFreeEffort()` clears Redis's 64-element threshold, so `UNLINK` really does defer the free). A separate process pings Redis every ~1 ms throughout; cleanup is then invoked via `cleanup_redis_storage`. | Metric | DEL (baseline) | UNLINK (this change) | |---|---|---| | Cleanup wall time | 968.8 / 996.4 / 953.7 ms | **3.4 / 7.3 / 5.3 ms** | | **Max PING RTT during cleanup** | **965.4 / 993.2 / 950.2 ms** | **1.30 / 0.55 / 2.19 ms** | | PINGs completed during cleanup | 3 / 3 / 3 | 3 / 5 / 4 | | PINGs *expected* at baseline rate | 644 / 652 / 641 | 2.3 / 4.9 / 3.5 | | `used_memory` when cleanup returned | 1.2 MB | **351.4 / 350.3 / 350.8 MB** | | `lazyfree_pending_objects` | 0 | **1** | Baseline (quiet) PING latency for reference: p50 ≈ 0.35 ms, p99 ≈ 0.62 ms. The completion shortfall is what confirms the mechanism: at the observed baseline rate the sampler should have completed ~645 pings during a ~970 ms window and completed **3** — Redis served ~0.5 % of the requests it otherwise would have. Under `UNLINK` the completed count matches the prediction (3 vs 2.3, 5 vs 4.9, 4 vs 3.5); the server never stopped serving. Deferred reclamation is directly observable: when `UNLINK` cleanup returns the keys are gone from the keyspace but `used_memory` is still ~350 MB with `lazyfree_pending_objects` = 1. This is the operator-visible behavior documented in the KubeRay GCS-FT guide, and the reason the escape hatch exists. 351 MB is a modest GCS table by production standards. The stall scales with the size of the freed value; `UNLINK`'s main-thread cost does not — it is an O(1) keyspace unlink regardless of hash size. #### Benchmark 2: SCAN round trips **Workload.** 200,000 unrelated keys sharing the instance (other Ray clusters or other applications) plus one 5-key namespace. Master's behavior is reproduced exactly by setting `RAY_maximum_gcs_storage_operation_batch_size=10` (`COUNT 10` ≡ the server default), so both arms again run the same binary. | Metric | master (`COUNT` 10) | this change (`COUNT` 1000) | Improvement | |---|---|---|---| | `SCAN` round trips | 19,272 | **200** | **96×** fewer | | Cleanup wall time | 2441.7 ms | **121.8 ms** | **20×** faster | | Server CPU in `SCAN` (`INFO commandstats`) | 188,669 µs | **84,205 µs** | **2.2×** less | Total *server* CPU spent in `SCAN` also drops by more than half, so raising `COUNT` is not trading server work for fewer round trips — at `COUNT 10` the per-call overhead (command parse, reply construction, event-loop turn) dominates the actual bucket scanning. This also bounds the risk of a larger `COUNT`: it raises per-call server work from ~10 to ~1000 buckets, but the measured per-call cost is 84,205 µs / 200 ≈ **0.42 ms** — three orders of magnitude below the ~950 ms `DEL` stall this change removes, and it blocks nothing longer than a normal command. #### Methodology notes Recording these because they are easy to get wrong, and the first numbers I produced were wrong for both reasons: 1. **An in-process sampler measures the GIL, not Redis.** `cleanup_redis_storage` is a synchronous Cython → C++ call that holds the GIL for its entire duration, so a sampler running as a *thread* of the benchmark process is starved by the GIL rather than by Redis, and the stall it reports cannot be attributed to the Redis main thread. The sampler must be a separate **process**, correlating with the driver via absolute `time.time()` stamps. 2. **Bucketing samples by completion time hides the stall.** A ping issued before cleanup starts and answered after it ends — precisely the sample that spans the stall — gets misfiled as "after", producing `during_max = null`. Samples must be bucketed by *overlap* with the cleanup window. Neither affects Benchmark 2 (server-side counters from `INFO commandstats`, independent of the client), nor the `cleanup_wall_ms`, `used_memory`, or `lazyfree_pending_objects` figures in Benchmark 1. Incidental: `DEBUG POPULATE` is disabled by default in Redis 7 (`enable-debug-command`), so filler keys are written with pipelined `SET`. #### Reproduction ```bash # Standalone Redis 7.2.3 (Ray's bundled binary) python/ray/core/src/ray/thirdparty/redis/src/redis-server \ --port 6399 --bind 127.0.0.1 --save '' --appendonly no --loglevel warning & # Benchmark 1 (per arm, separate processes) RAY_redis_namespace_cleanup_use_unlink=0 python bench_latency.py 6399 del 1000000 256 RAY_redis_namespace_cleanup_use_unlink=1 python bench_latency.py 6399 unlink 1000000 256 # Benchmark 2 RAY_maximum_gcs_storage_operation_batch_size=10 python bench_scan.py 6399 master-COUNT10 200000 python bench_scan.py 6399 COUNT1000 200000 ```
